title: Palma to Bugia: the Wheels of the Art, the Missions to Islam, and the Stoning
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Palma, the Seneschal and the Poet

stops.name: Palma, birth into the merchant patriciate
stops.campa: Ramon is born in the City of Majorca, Palma, some three years after King James the Conqueror wrested the island from its Almohad governor and parceled its lands among the Catalan lords who financed the conquest. His father, Ramon Amat Llull, a Barcelona patrician granted estates in the new kingdom, raises him among the first Christian generation to call the island home. The boy grows up trilingual in the tongues of the conquered city, Catalan, Latin, and the Arabic still spoken in its markets, an inheritance that will outlast every other thing given him in this childhood.
suggested_refs: The old city walls and Almudaina of Palma, seat of the new Christian kingdom of Majorca into which Llull was born

stops.name: Palma, seneschal at the court of King James II, and the marriage to Blanca Picany
stops.campa: Grown to manhood, Ramon rises to seneschal of the household of the young Infante James, soon to be crowned first king of an independent Majorca, ordering the prince's table, his hunts, and his festivals. In this same year he marries Blanca Picany, a woman of good Majorcan family, and she will bear him two children, Domènec and Magdalena. He is, by every account left of these years, a man given wholly to the court: composing love verses in the vernacular, dressing richly, and pursuing, the chroniclers will not blush to say later, more than one lady not his wife.
suggested_refs: The royal palace of the Almudaina, Palma, seat of the household Llull served as seneschal
sources: J.N. Hillgarth, Ramon Lull and Lullism in Fourteenth-Century France

stops.name: Palma, the church of Santa Eulàlia, the horse ridden to the altar
stops.campa: The tradition of Majorca keeps a scene from these last worldly years: Ramon, hot in pursuit of a lady named in later memory Ambrosia de Castello, spurs his horse through the very doors of the church of Santa Eulàlia and up the nave toward the altar rail where she kneels at Mass, scattering the congregation to make his declaration before God and the parish. She does not receive him as a suitor. Instead, within the year, she opens her bodice and shows him a breast eaten half away by cancer, asking how he can desire a body so soon to be food for worms.
suggested_refs: The parish church of Santa Eulàlia, Palma, where the ride to the altar rail is remembered
sources: Tradition recorded in early vitae and local Majorcan memory (18th-c. hagiographies)
National Catholic Register, 'An Almost Patron Saint for Christian-Muslim Relations'

segments.name: The Five Visions and the Turning

stops.name: Palma, his chamber, the first vision of the Crucified
stops.campa: One night, sitting beside his bed to compose in his own vulgar tongue a song for a lady he loves with what he will later call a foolish love, Ramon looks up and to his right and sees Our Lord Jesus Christ hanging upon the Cross, suspended as if in mid-air within the chamber. He is thrown into terror and cannot finish the verse; he sets the pen aside and goes to sleep troubled. But when he takes up the same unfinished song some days after, the vision comes again in the same place and the same posture, and he understands it will not let him alone.
stops.quote: he looked to his right and saw our Lord Jesus Christ on the Cross, as if suspended in mid-air
stops.quote_source: Vita Coetanea (dictated at Paris, c. 1311; trans. Bonner)
suggested_refs: The Breviculum (Karlsruhe, Badische Landesbibliothek), whose illuminations depict the five visions of the Crucified

stops.name: Palma, the fifth vision and the three resolves
stops.campa: The vision returns three times more, at intervals of days, each time finding him at the same chamber, the same unfinished song. By the fifth appearance he no longer doubts its meaning and lies awake turning the matter until dawn: that God wills him to leave the world entirely. From that long night he draws three resolves that will govern every road left to him: to give his life for God's love and honor; to bring about, even at the cost of death, the conversion of the Saracens; and to write the best book in the world against the errors of unbelief.
stops.quote: to give up his soul for the sake of God's love and honor, to convert the Saracens to Christianity, and write the best book in the world against the errors of the unbelievers
suggested_refs: The Vita Coetanea itself, Llull's dictated autobiography naming these three resolves

stops.name: Palma, the feast of Saint Francis, the goods sold
stops.campa: Three months Ramon turns the vision over before he acts. Then, on the feast of Saint Francis, he hears a bishop preach in the Franciscan church of Palma on how Francis abandoned everything he owned to follow Christ, and the sermon finishes what the five visions began. He resolves that same day to sell his goods, setting aside only what Blanca and the children will need to live, and to leave his house. He goes among the poor and the churches of the city rather than the halls of the court; not yet to his wife's bed or his children's table to say farewell, for that leave-taking still waits.
stops.quote: to sell his goods, leaving the amount necessary for the upkeep of his family, and to leave his home
suggested_refs: The Franciscan church of Palma and the feast of Saint Francis, 4 October, on which Llull's decision is placed

stops.name: Rocamadour, before the Black Virgin
stops.campa: The first road out of the world takes Ramon north into Quercy, to the cliff-shrine of Rocamadour, where the ancient black-carved Virgin looks down from her chapel cut into the rock above the gorge of the Alzou, and the sword of Roland, they say, still hangs on the wall where it was thrown. He kneels before this Virgin and lays his charge at her feet: that his three resolves might not fail for want of learning, since a man who does not know the tongues and reasons of the Saracens can convert no one by will alone.
suggested_refs: The Black Madonna of Rocamadour and the sword said to be Durendal, relics of the cliff shrine named first among Llull's pilgrimages
sources: Vita Coetanea, ch. 2 (Rocamadour named before Compostela)

stops.name: The road to Santiago de Compostela
stops.campa: From Rocamadour the pilgrim road carries him west across Christian Spain to the shrine of Saint James in Galicia, one pilgrim among the thousands who cross the peninsula each year on the same errand. He goes begging his bread, seeking at the tomb of the apostle a confirmation of the great task the visions have laid on him: to spend himself entirely, and to find some means of turning unbelievers by reason rather than the sword, since reason, unlike the sword, can be carried into the very heart of the enemy's own house.
suggested_refs: The Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela and the shell-badge of Saint James, insignia of the pilgrim road Llull walked
sources: Vita Coetanea, ch. 2 (his pilgrimages named among his early penitential acts)

segments.name: Nine Years of Arabic, the Slave, and the Mountain

stops.name: Barcelona and Palma, Penyafort's counsel and the purchase of the Moorish slave
stops.campa: Coming back through Barcelona, Ramon puts to the aged Dominican Ramon de Penyafort his plan to study at Paris, and is talked out of it: the old canonist persuades him to go home to Majorca instead and learn what he needs there. Obedient, he puts on a habit of the coarsest cloth he can find and buys a Muslim slave in the Palma market to teach him Arabic, the language in which his great book against unbelief must first be argued if it is ever to reach a Saracen ear. For nine years master and slave sit together over the grammar and the Qur'an, the convert schooled daily by the man he owns.
suggested_refs: The Arabic grammars and glossaries Llull is recorded as compiling in these years of study

stops.name: Palma, the Book of Contemplation begun
stops.campa: In the middle years of this long study Ramon begins the vast Book of Contemplation in God, writing it first, by his own later account, in Arabic before recasting it in Catalan: a summa in some four hundred chapters surveying the whole of creation as a ladder of ascent toward its Maker, chapter answering chapter in a strict numerical architecture he will use again and again. He also compiles a compendium of al-Ghazali's logic for his own use, absorbing the very tools of Arabic dialectic he means one day to turn back against the faith that shaped them.
suggested_refs: Llibre de contemplació en Déu, Llull's vast early summa, drafted first in Arabic
sources: Anthony Bonner, The Art and Logic of Ramon Llull

stops.name: Palma, the slave's blasphemy and the noose
stops.campa: The long partnership ends in catastrophe. The slave, hearing his master name Christ, blasphemes against him; Ramon, in a fury he will spend the rest of his life regretting, strikes the man across the face. The slave, in terror of the punishment sure to follow a hand raised against his master, gets a knife and wounds Ramon before he is overpowered and thrown into a cell to await judgment. There, before any sentence is passed, he hangs himself with his own belt. Ramon is left with his Arabic, his grief, and a first hard lesson in how far short of his own resolve a man may fall.
suggested_refs: The episode as Llull himself dictates it in the Vita Coetanea, the one place his own violence, not the world's, breaks something
sources: J.N. Hillgarth, Ramon Lull and Lullism

stops.name: Puig de Randa, the retreat and the illumination
stops.campa: Grieved and shaken, Ramon climbs the small hard mountain called Puig de Randa in the middle of the island, to a hermitage cut into its slope, meaning to spend some days wholly in contemplation. Turning the great labor of his life over yet again in solitary prayer, he is answered: in an instant, without warning, the Lord illuminates his understanding entirely, showing him at one stroke the form and method by which the book against unbelief must be built: letters, figures, and turning wheels sufficient to demonstrate every truth of the faith by reason alone. He stays eight days more on the mountain before trusting himself to come down.
stops.quote: the Lord suddenly illuminated his mind, giving him the form and method for writing the aforementioned book against the errors of the unbelievers
suggested_refs: The Santuari de Cura atop Puig de Randa, built on the traditional site of the illumination, and the wheel-diagrams of the Ars generalis it commemorates
sources: Qui és Ramon Llull, 'Illumination at Randa'

stops.name: La Real, the abbey of the grey monks, the Art set down
stops.campa: Coming down from Randa, Ramon does not go home but to the nearby Cistercian abbey of La Real, outside Palma, and asks the monks for a cell and ink. There, before the illumination can fade, he sets down the first version of what he calls the Ars compendiosa inveniendi veritatem, the Brief Art of Finding Truth, built on the great circling Figure A, whose letters spell out the Dignities of God, Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, Power, Wisdom, and the rest, turning against one another on concentric wheels to generate, mechanically and without appeal to authority, every proof the missionary's tongue will need.
suggested_refs: Figure A of the Ars, the wheel of the Dignities of God, root diagram of every later version of Llull's Art
sources: Anthony Bonner, The Art and Logic of Ramon Llull
Umberto Eco, 'The Ars Magna by Ramon Llull'

stops.name: Montpellier, summoned by the young King of Majorca
stops.campa: James II, newly enthroned as king of an independent Majorca and already Ramon's acquaintance from the seneschal years, summons him to his court in exile at Montpellier, the mainland city that is half capital to the island kingdom. Here Ramon lays before the king the whole of his design: the Art now written, and beyond it a plan for a house where friars might learn Arabic before ever setting foot among the Saracens, so the sermon might follow directly on the grammar lesson. James, moved by the argument or by old loyalty to his former servant, takes the plan to heart and to Rome.
suggested_refs: The royal palace of the kings of Majorca at Montpellier, seat of James II's mainland court

stops.name: Miramar, the monastery of tongues confirmed by Rome
stops.campa: On the cliff road between Valldemossa and Deià, above the sea, King James founds the monastery he and Ramon have planned: Miramar, house of thirteen Franciscan brothers set apart to do nothing but learn Arabic, so missionaries might go out at last equipped with the very tongue of those they mean to turn. On the seventeenth of October Pope John XXI signs the bull confirming the foundation and its royal endowment. It is the first working piece of Ramon's three resolves made real in stone and rule, a decade after the visions in his chamber, and it will outlast the century.
suggested_refs: The papal bull of Pope John XXI, 17 October 1276, confirming Miramar; the surviving monastery on the Valldemossa-Deià road

stops.name: Montpellier, Blanquerna and the Ars demonstrativa
stops.campa: Settled for a season at Montpellier, Ramon writes a longer and more rigorous version of his system, the Ars demonstrativa, and beside it something stranger: a novel, Blanquerna, following a man who rises from hermit to pope and then renounces even the papacy to return to solitude, the first romance of its kind in a vernacular tongue built to carry philosophy inside a story. Within its last book he sets a separate treatise, the Book of the Lover and the Beloved, mystical verses in the voice of a soul in love with God, as many, the book declares of itself, as the year has days.
stops.quote: The Lover asked his Beloved if there remained in Him anything still to be loved.
stops.quote_source: The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, verse 1 (within Blaquerna, Pt. V; trans. E. Allison Peers, 1923)
suggested_refs: Blanquerna and its embedded Book of the Lover and the Beloved, Llull's most read mystical work
sources: E. Allison Peers, trans., The Book of the Lover and the Beloved

stops.name: Rome, the first audience, a dead pope
stops.campa: Ramon crosses to Rome to bring his whole design before the Holy See itself: the Art, the language schools, and beyond them a plan for the recovery of the Holy Land by preaching rather than only the sword. He arrives to find Pope Honorius IV dead and no successor yet seated, the curia scattered and unable to hear so large a petition from an unbeneficed layman of Majorca with no order and no title behind his name. He waits as long as he can afford, then turns north, carrying his papers and his patience to a university that will at least always sit still to argue.
suggested_refs: The vacant Apostolic See of 1287, the first of several papacies whose deaths or indifference Llull's petitions outlived

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne, Felix and the doctors of the schools
stops.campa: At the end of the year Ramon reaches Paris and lodges near the schools of the Left Bank, frequenting the halls of the Sorbonne where he will be tolerated, argued with, and occasionally admired for the next twenty years of visits. Here he composes Felix, or the Book of Wonders, sending a wandering fool through the length of the created world, animal, vegetable, celestial, and human, to ask at every turn why things are as they are, wringing a small treatise on natural philosophy from a boy's naive questions. Doctors of the university, Peter of Limoges among them, begin to gather around his figures and wheels.
suggested_refs: The medieval Sorbonne quarter of Paris, and Llull's Felix, or the Book of Wonders, composed on this first stay

stops.name: Montpellier, the Art simplified, the friars' recommendation
stops.campa: Back at Montpellier through 1289 and into 1290, Ramon labors to cut his system down to a form students can actually hold in the memory, paring the great early Art toward what will become, after further revision, the Ars generalis ultima and its short companion the Ars brevis. The Franciscan order, whose habit and rule he has followed without formal vows since his conversion, commends his teaching to those who would learn it. He is close now to sixty, unbeneficed still, without a see or a chair, entirely dependent on the goodwill of princes and the patience of scholars for every road ahead.
suggested_refs: Successive redactions of the Art at Montpellier, converging on the Ars brevis and Ars generalis ultima of 1308
sources: Anthony Bonner, The Art and Logic of Ramon Llull

segments.name: Genoa and the First Mission to Tunis

stops.name: Genoa, the terror on the quay, the ship not boarded
stops.campa: In Genoa, waiting on a berth for Tunis, the mission he has planned and postponed for thirty years since the visions in his chamber, Ramon is seized by a terror he had not foreseen: that he will be caught on landing and rot the rest of his days in a Saracen prison, or die at once, unremembered and without the sermon he crossed the sea to preach. Feverish and shaking, he books passage on the first galley out and then, at the very quay, cannot make himself climb aboard; his friends, seeing him ill, hold him back from a ship he was in any case too broken to sail on.
suggested_refs: The medieval port of Genoa, staging ground for every Lullian crossing to North Africa
sources: IEMed, 'Ramon Llull and his Islamic Undertaking'

stops.name: Genoa, the fever breaks, a new ship taken in secret
stops.campa: The fever and the terror pass, as fevers do, and within the year Ramon recovers his resolve along with his health. He books a second passage, and this time tells no one, not even the friends who kept him from the first ship, boarding before dawn so no hand of affection can hold him back again. He is past sixty, has never in his life crossed to Africa, and knows exactly, from the terror already lived through once, what he is sailing toward; he sails anyway, judging a coward's death by inches worse than whatever waits in Tunis.
suggested_refs: The Vita Coetanea's own account of this second, secret departure, the turning point of the Tunis mission

stops.name: Tunis, the challenge to the doctors of the law
stops.campa: Ramon lands at Tunis in September and, once his Arabic has drawn a circle of the city's learned men around him, throws down a wager few missionaries before him have dared: let the doctors of Muslim law bring their strongest arguments, and if they can answer his reasons and convince him of the truth of Islam, he will become a Muslim on the spot. It is the whole logic of the Art turned outward into the street, argument alone, without a soldier behind it, staking his own soul on the wheels of the Dignities holding firm against the sharpest minds Tunis can set against them.
suggested_refs: The Disputatio Raymundi Christiani et Sarraceni and related Lullian treatises modeled on this Tunis wager
sources: IEMed, 'Ramon Llull and his Islamic Undertaking'

stops.name: Tunis, the public sermon, the death sentence commuted
stops.campa: Emboldened, or perhaps only faithful past the point of prudence, Ramon goes on to preach the Christian faith openly in the streets, a plain breach of the peace between the two kingdoms, which forbids preaching against Islam on Muslim ground. He is seized, beaten, and condemned by the emir to death by the sword. Only the intervention of the city's own mufti, together with resident Catalan and Genoese merchants who plead the value of peaceful trade over one troublesome friar's head, turns the sentence aside; he is expelled instead of beheaded, put aboard a ship under guard and told never to return.
suggested_refs: The medina of Tunis and its Hafsid court, site of the first of three commuted death sentences Llull would face in North Africa
sources: IEMed, 'Ramon Llull and his Islamic Undertaking'

stops.name: Naples, cast ashore, expelled
stops.campa: The guard-ship puts Ramon ashore at Naples in October, alive against the odds he had reckoned in Genoa the year before, his first African mission ended in expulsion rather than the martyrdom he had half expected and, by his own later admission, almost wished for. He does not go home to Majorca to recover but stays in the bustling Angevin port, taking up his pen again almost at once, already turning the failure at Tunis into material for the next version of his Art and the next appeal to whatever pope will next sit on the vacant throne of Rome.
suggested_refs: Angevin Naples, way-station and refuge after every one of Llull's African expulsions

segments.name: Rome, Paris, and the Furthest East

stops.name: Rome, two years of writing, the Desconhort
stops.campa: Ramon settles in Rome through 1295 and into 1296, working the halls of a curia that has cycled through Celestine V's brief and disastrous reign into Boniface VIII's, petitioning each in turn for language schools, for a standing military order to hold the Holy Land, for anything at all beyond the polite hearing every clerk in Rome has learned to give him. Out of the frustration of these years he writes the Desconhort, the Book of Discomfort, a bitter dialogue between an old fool and a hermit who tells him bluntly that no one will ever believe his Art was given him by God.
suggested_refs: The Desconhort, Llull's poem of self-doubt written amid the indifference of the Roman curia

stops.name: Paris, the second stay, the war on Averroes
stops.campa: Ramon returns to Paris in August, this time to fight a battle he judges as dangerous to Christendom as any Saracen sword: the teaching, inside the very faculty of arts he had once courted for allies, of Averroist doctrines holding that reason and revealed faith may each be true on their own separate terms, with no need to reconcile them. Against this Ramon sets treatise after treatise arguing, by the Art's own mechanism, that faith and reason are one necessary demonstration and cannot be split apart, a fight he will return to Paris to renew twice more in the years still left him.
suggested_refs: The Latin Averroist controversy at the University of Paris, target of Llull's Paris writings from 1298 onward

stops.name: Barcelona, the king's license to preach in synagogue and mosque
stops.campa: Home again in the Crown of Aragon, Ramon obtains from King James II a document few missionaries before him have carried: royal license to enter the synagogues and mosques of the king's own realms and preach there directly to Jews and Muslims living under Christian rule, compelling their attendance if need be. It is the domestic twin of the African missions, proof that Ramon's design was never only for the distant Saracen but for the unconverted living inside Christendom's own cities, and it gives legal shelter to years of preaching he will carry out in Barcelona, Valencia, and Majorca between the longer voyages abroad.
suggested_refs: The royal license of James II of Aragon (1299) authorizing Llull to preach in synagogues and mosques of the realm

stops.name: Majorca, the Cant de Ramon, the old man's own accounting
stops.campa: Home on the island through a long quiet year, Ramon writes the Cant de Ramon, fourteen stanzas of six eight-syllable lines that walk his whole life past the reader: the conversion, Miramar, the Art, the roads and the refusals. It is the troubadour craft of his worldly youth taken up again and turned to the only lady he now serves, and it is not a boast. He complains in it, plainly, of how little his labor has come to, and asks God for protection and for intelligent companions to carry the work he cannot carry alone much longer.
suggested_refs: The Cant de Ramon (1300), Llull's autobiographical poem in fourteen stanzas, the troubadour form turned to his own account
sources: Qui és Ramon Llull, 'Cant de Ramon'

stops.name: Cyprus, Famagusta, the mission to the Latin East
stops.campa: Nearing seventy, Ramon takes ship again, this time east to Cyprus, last major Christian foothold within easy reach of the Levant, its port of Famagusta thick with Genoese, Venetian, and Frankish merchants trading into a Mamluk-held Holy Land no crusader army now holds. He preaches among the mixed Latin, Greek, and Syrian population of the island, tests his Art on whatever learned Muslims and schismatic Christians pass through the port, and begins to press the case, which will occupy his last decade, for a mission to the Tatar khans of the Asian mainland, whose conversion he believes might outflank Islam entirely.
suggested_refs: The Genoese and Venetian merchant quarters of Lusignan Famagusta, Llull's base for this eastern mission

stops.name: Port Ayas, the Armenian coast, the embassy to the Tatars
stops.campa: From Cyprus Ramon crosses to Port Ayas on the Cilician coast, the chief harbor of the Christian kingdom of Lesser Armenia and the western terminus of the overland road to the court of the Ilkhan in Persia, where embassies and merchants pass constantly between the Mongol world and the Latin one. Here, closer to the Tatars than any earlier stage of his life has brought him, he composes the Rhetorica nova, an art of persuasion meant to travel with missionaries as far as the steppe itself, before turning back west, his hope of reaching the Great Khan's own court still years, and several voyages, away.
suggested_refs: Port Ayas (Yumurtalık), gateway of Cilician Armenia to the Mongol Ilkhanate, and Llull's Rhetorica nova written there

stops.name: Montpellier, between missions, the Book of the End
stops.campa: Back on the Montpellier road after Genoa, Ramon writes the Liber de fine, the Book of the End, laying out in cold administrative detail exactly how a crusade ought to be financed, manned, and directed if Christendom would only listen: standing military orders merged into one, a tithe on the clergy, a fleet built and kept ready rather than raised anew for each disaster. He is past seventy and has buried, in these same years, most of the popes and princes he first petitioned as a younger man; still he drafts the plan again, on the theory that the right argument, offered often enough, must eventually find the right ear.
suggested_refs: Liber de fine, Llull's late crusade-planning treatise, one of dozens of such petitions addressed to Rome and the courts of Europe

stops.name: Bugia, the public sermon, the stones and the chains
stops.campa: Now past seventy-five, Ramon sails to Bugia on the Barbary coast and, as at Tunis fourteen years before, preaches the Trinity openly in the public square. A mob gathers, stones him where he stands, and drags him before the qadi, who this time does not commute the sentence to expulsion outright but has him chained and thrown into a cell for half a year, debating faith through the bars with a Muslim scholar the Latin calls Homer in an exchange he will later set down as the Disputatio Raymundi christiani et Homeri saraceni, before the city's authorities finally put the old man on a ship bound home.
suggested_refs: The Disputatio Raymundi christiani et Homeri saraceni, Llull's account of the prison debates at Bugia
sources: Christianity Today, 'Christians & Muslims: A Gallery of Spiritual Warriors'

stops.name: At sea, the wreck off Pisa
stops.campa: The homeward ship from Bugia founders in a storm within sight of the Tuscan coast; Ramon, chained by age and weakness now as much as by any Saracen jailer, is pulled from the wreck along with what survivors the sea allows and put ashore near Pisa rather than at Genoa or Majorca as intended. He has survived a death sentence, a half-year's imprisonment, and a shipwreck within the space of two years, and takes the accumulation, as he has taken every earlier trial since the visions in his chamber, as proof that his work is not yet finished and God is not yet done with him.
suggested_refs: The Tuscan coast near Pisa, landfall of the wrecked Bugia return voyage

stops.name: Pisa, the Ars brevis finished, the crusade renewed
stops.campa: Recovering at Pisa, Ramon puts the Art into its final and most compact form, the Ars generalis ultima and its short companion the Ars brevis, the version students after him will actually use, having pared away four decades of revision to the working core of the wheels and the Dignities. He also renews, from his sickbed, the old campaign for a new crusade, addressing the Pisan authorities and any Genoese captain who will listen, unwilling to let a shipwreck stand as the last word on a plan for the Holy Land he first drafted for Pope Nicholas IV twenty years before.
suggested_refs: Ars brevis (Pisa, 1308), the final compact version of the Art still read and taught today
sources: Anthony Bonner, The Art and Logic of Ramon Llull

segments.name: Paris, Vienne, and the Universal Council

stops.name: Montpellier, the crusade treatise renewed
stops.campa: Back at Montpellier, Ramon drafts yet another crusade memorandum, this one timed for the general council Pope Clement V has summoned and twice postponed, where Ramon means to be heard whenever it finally sits. He is seventy-seven, has been refused by popes and princes across four decades, and shows in these last petitions no sign of the fatigue his body must by now be carrying; the wheels of the Art, he insists to whoever will still hear him, prove the case for the recovery of the Holy Land as certainly as they prove any article of the Trinity.
suggested_refs: Clement V's bull Regnans in coelis summoning the general council, the hearing Llull's late memoranda were written for

stops.name: Paris, the last stay, thirty works, the doctors' approval
stops.campa: Ramon returns to Paris in November for what will be his longest and most productive stay, dictating some thirty treatises against Averroism and in defense of the Art over two years. In February of 1310 the masters of arts and medicine, for the first time in his long acquaintance with the schools, put their names to a letter certifying his teaching as sound; the chancellor follows the year after, declaring the Lullian doctrine in accord with the Catholic faith, and King Philip the Fair writes commending him. It is the nearest thing to victory Ramon will ever have from a university that argued with him for twenty years.
suggested_refs: The Paris masters' letter of February 1310 and the chancellor's certification of 1311, the only academic endorsement Llull's Art ever won in his lifetime

stops.name: Vienne, the Council, the chairs of tongues decreed
stops.campa: At seventy-nine Ramon travels to the general council convened at Vienne on the Rhône, carrying the same petition he has carried to every pope since Honorius IV: chairs of Hebrew, Arabic, and Aramaic founded at the great universities, so missionaries need never again cross the sea as unprepared as he once did. This time the council agrees, decreeing such chairs for Rome, Bologna, Oxford, Paris, and Salamanca. It is the clearest fulfillment, in his own lifetime, of the second of his three resolves from the chamber in Palma nearly fifty years before: that the tongues of the unbeliever be taught rather than merely fought.
suggested_refs: The decree of the Council of Vienne (1311-12) founding chairs of Hebrew, Arabic, and Aramaic, Llull's decades-long petition realized

stops.name: Majorca, the will dictated
stops.campa: Home in Majorca, Ramon sets his worldly affairs in order, dictating a will that disposes of his remaining property and, among its provisions, leaves funds for the copying and circulation of his books, the nearest thing to an archive he can arrange for a body of work numbering by now well past two hundred titles in Catalan, Arabic, and Latin. He is over eighty, has outlived his wife, and spent the family inheritance decades ago on the missions and the schools; what he leaves behind is paper, wheels of letters, and a design still incomplete, since no pope has yet sent the crusade or the missionaries he asked for.
suggested_refs: Llull's will of 26 April 1313, providing for the preservation and copying of his written corpus

segments.name: The Last Mission and the Sea

stops.name: Messina, the wait for passage
stops.campa: Rather than settle into the retirement his will implies, Ramon crosses to Sicily and waits at Messina under the protection of King Frederick III, seeking a ship and a sponsor for one more crossing to North Africa. He is over eighty and has already survived a death sentence, a half-year's chains, and a shipwreck on the same coast he now means to sail toward a fourth time; those around him, the Vita Coetanea admits without softening it, think him an old man courting a death he has no need to seek so directly, and say so to his face.
suggested_refs: Messina under Frederick III of Sicily, staging point for Llull's final African crossing

stops.name: Tunis, the last mission, eighty-two years old
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of August Ramon sails again for Tunis, drawn this time by report that the Hafsid ruler himself has shown some private leaning toward the Christian faith and might, with the right argument pressed at the right hour, be brought to it openly. He goes first quietly, seeking out and strengthening the small community of Christian merchants and converts already living under Hafsid rule before he risks anything more public, an old missionary's patience learned across four decades of expulsions, patient in a way the young man who rode his horse into Santa Eulàlia's nave never once managed to be.
suggested_refs: Hafsid Tunis under al-Lihyani, target of Llull's fourth and final North African mission

stops.name: Tunis, the secret strengthening of the converts
stops.campa: Ramon spends the months of this last year in the quiet work, meeting secretly with converts and wavering Christians in Tunis to hold their faith steady, gathering strength, by every account, for one open act of witness before the end. It is the long patient road the Book of the Lover and the Beloved had already named for him decades before at Montpellier, a road he now walks in fact rather than only in verse, and knows by this stage of his life exactly where such a road in this country tends to lead.
stops.quote: Long and perilous are the paths by which the Lover seeks his Beloved. They are peopled by cares, sighs and tears. They are lit up by love.
stops.quote_source: The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, verse 2 (trans. E. Allison Peers, 1923)
suggested_refs: Hafsid Tunis, where Llull's own dated pages place him through the whole of 1315
sources: Christian History Institute, 'Ramon Lull: From Erotic Poet to Ecstatic Mystic and Eager Martyr'

stops.name: Tunis, the last book, December 1315
stops.campa: In December, in his eighty-fourth year and in a Muslim city where preaching his faith aloud is a capital matter, Ramon finishes another book and dates it, as he has dated books for fifty years, with the place and the month. It is the last page of a working life that has run past two hundred and fifty titles in Catalan, Arabic, and Latin, and it is written in Tunis. Nothing in it takes leave of anything. He is still arguing, still numbering his figures, still setting down the wheels for whoever comes after to turn.
suggested_refs: Llull's last dated work, Tunis, December 1315, the final page of the corpus
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ramon Llull' (his last work is dated December 1315 in Tunis)

stops.name: Bugia, the public preaching, the stoning of the mob
stops.campa: The tradition of his cult carries him back to Bugia for the end, the city of his earlier chains, and there Ramon steps into the open square and preaches the Trinity as plainly as he preached it at Tunis in 1293. This time no mufti intervenes and no qadi commutes a sentence: the mob, roused past any authority's control, stones him where he stands and leaves him for dead in the street. Genoese merchants find him still breathing among the stones, carry him to their ship, and put out to sea for Majorca before the city can finish what it started.
suggested_refs: The traditional site of Llull's stoning in the public square of Bugia (Béjaïa), commemorated in his later cult as a martyr's death
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ramon Llull' (the sources name Bougie or Tunis; the cult keeps Bougie)

stops.name: The sea off Mallorca, death within sight of home
stops.campa: The Genoese ship makes slow way toward Majorca with its half-dead passenger, and the island itself, they say, is in sight from the deck, the hills above Palma visible on the horizon where Ramon was born eighty-four years before beside the same water, when he dies of the stoning's wounds without setting foot again on his own shore. Asked once, in his own book, where a soul in love with God is going and where it comes from, he had already written the only answer that will now serve as his epitaph.
stops.quote: They said to the Lover: 'Whither goest thou?' He answered: 'I come from my Beloved.' 'Whence comest thou?' 'I go to my Beloved.' 'When wilt thou return?' 'I shall be with my Beloved.' 'How long wilt thou be with thy Beloved?' 'As long as my thoughts remain on Him.'
stops.quote_source: The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, verse 24 (trans. E. Allison Peers, 1923)
suggested_refs: The traditional account of Llull's death at sea within sight of Majorca, spring 1316
sources: Rutas Ramon Llull, 'Last will and death'

stops.name: Palma, the tomb in the basilica of Sant Francesc
stops.campa: They bring Ramon's body ashore at Palma, the city of his birth, his seneschal years, his visions, and his horse ridden into Santa Eulàlia's nave, and bury him among the Franciscans whose habit he wore without vows for over fifty years, in the church of Sant Francesc. His alabaster tomb, raised more than a century later, will show him lying in the habit still, ringed by scenes from a life the Church will one day call blessed martyrdom and the university men of Paris and Barcelona will keep reading, wheel by turning wheel, for as long as there are wheels left to turn.
suggested_refs: The alabaster tomb of Ramon Llull (1448) in the Basilica of Sant Francesc, Palma, his final resting place
sources: Raco.cat, 'Ramon Llull Cloister of the Church of Sant Francesc, Palma de Mallorca'
